_exec_summary.SummaryText:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

A.	Process description & regulated substance

The Kraft Heinz Foods Davenport, IA plant manufactures or produces meat products. The NAICS code for the primary process at this facility is 311612. This facility is capable of producing and packaging various bologna, ham, turkey, beef, chicken, and pork products for consumer intake. Many areas of the plant are equipped with refrigeration systems to preserve meat products. Some of these areas include coolers and chill cells. Kraft Heinz Foods has one regulated substance, anhydrous ammonia (CAS 7664-41-7), under 40 CFR 68, at the Davenport Plant. Ammonia is used as a refrigerant in the plants chilling system. The total ammonia charge, at the Davenport Plant, is approximately 33,000 pounds. Thus, 40 CFR 68 is applicable to Kraft Foods in Davenport. The ammonia threshold for triggering applicability to 40 CFR 68 is 10,000 pounds.  The EHS manager (Lisa Culberson) is responsible for development, implementation, and integration of the risk management program elements. 

B.	Release prevention & emergency response policy

The Davenport Plant has implemented an electronic preventive maintenance system (SAP) that uses weekly batched data to track training and inspection dates and issues reminders to responsible groups.

The emergency response policies at this facility ensure that there is emergency response coverage for the plant during the continual 24 hrs and 7 day plant operations. The Davenport Fire Department is contacted in the event of an emergency and is trained in paramedical services. The Davenport Facility also has a thorough emergency training program for on-site emergency responders. Selected employees have completed 24 hours of formal emergency response training. These employees are considered Hazardous Material Technicians.
*From this point in the Executive Summary, anhydrous ammonia will be synonymous with ammonia.
C.	Worst-case and Alternative Release Scenarios
The ammonia refrigeration system

has associated hazards that can potentially affect on-site employees, and the general public off-site, if there is a release from the system. Although the alternative release scenario is more probable, the US EPA requires that one worst-case and one alternative release scenario be reported for each regulated chemical. 

Ammonia 
Ammonia is classified as a Group 2 Refrigerant per ASHRAE Standard 34-1989.  The dominant characteristic of this chemical is its toxicity.  It is a self-alarming chemical by its distinctive pungent odor.  Due to this odor, persons exposed to ammonia vapor will not voluntarily stay in areas of even small concentrations.  Ammonia is flammable in a very narrow and high range of concentration with a high ignition temperature.  It is not poisonous, but it is corrosive to human tissue.  Ammonia is readily absorbed into the moisture of the skin and, at high concentrations, can cause severe burns.
The risks to persons in an accidental release of ammonia include:
1.         Irritation of respiratory tract,
2.         Corrosive attack of skin and other tissue,
3.         Freezing of skin and other body tissue when contacted by liquid ammonia
4.         Death

Below is a description of the release scenarios for ammonia and their off-site consequences.  
(Maps are attached at the end)

           Worst-case scenario - The largest potential release of ammonia will occur with the largest vessel, located in the powerhouse.  The largest quantity of ammonia that can be stored in a vessel at our facility is in the engine room.  The total quantity of ammonia that is in this vessel is 9,700 pounds.  If punctured, it is assumed that 9,700 pounds is released to the atmosphere in 10 minutes.

Under Section 68.25(c)(1), a regulated toxic substance such as ammonia, which is normally a gas at ambient temperature and handled as a liquid under pressure, shall be considered to be released as a gas over a 10-minute period.  Thus, ammonias physical state in the worst-cas

e release is a gas. A wind speed of 1.5 m/s and an atmospheric stability class F was used for this scenario.  As well as ground level release per Appendix A 40 CFR Part 68.22.

           The ammonia worst case release scenario map was created using mapdevelopers.com - putting the radius of 1.8 miles (perimeter of 11.3 miles, area of 10.2 sq miles).  The toxic endpoint of 1.8 miles was determined by using the EPAs Appendix E: Supplemental Risk Management Program Guidelines for Ammonia Refrigeration Facilities. 

The estimated affected residential population is 1,700 people, and the facility is located in a rural area. It is classified as rural if there are less than 750 people per square kilometer, there are approximately 160 people per square kilometer surrounding the Davenport facility. The terrain around us is generally flat and unobstructed. The website used to obtain the population data was maps.ie. The list of affected receptors for both scenarios were obtained using Google maps and are listed in the Appendix.
Alternative Release Scenario - The worst-case release is less likely to occur than the following scenario.  The alternative release scenario that meets both selection criteria is an ammonia release from the tank in the pickle room.  A puncture in the tank produces a jet release at the hole.  The pickle tanks (3) are located indoors in the pickle room and the PRVs on these tanks discharge to the roof. There are no applicable administrative controls or passive mitigation. Active mitigation of the release is human intervention (PRVs shutdown at 10 minutes from the start of the release).  

Our calculations show that the ammonia vapor release rate is 20 lb/min for 10 minutes from the pickle tank that holds 200 pounds.

The ammonia alternative release scenario was mapped using mapdevelopers.com - putting the radius of .1 miles.  The release rate and toxic endpoint of .1 miles was determined by using the EPAs Appendix E: Supplemental Risk Management Program

Guidelines for Ammonia Refrigeration Facilities. A wind speed of 3 m/s and an atmospheric stability class D was used for this scenario. The list of affected receptors is in the Appendix. The estimated effected residential population is 0 people.

D.  General Accidental Release Prevention Program and Chemical-Specific Prevention Steps

The Davenport facility has developed an OSHA PSM program for their ammonia refrigeration system.  Ammonia falls under the RMP Program 3 prevention program, which is similar to the OSHA PSM program. If the process is in compliance with OSHA PSM, then it should be in compliance with RMP Program 3.  Thus, Krafts ammonia PSM has been reviewed and determined to be complete for the RMP document. The program is located on sharepoint and in the Ammonia Emergency Action Plan.

There are several aspects of the prevention program that are key:
1.         The new ammonia refrigeration system has been designed to provide sufficient guarding for the ammonia pipelines and equipment.
2.         The Davenport plant maintains good training, programs, and employee awareness of operating procedures. An annual Ammonia Mock Spill Drill occurs for emergency response procedures.
3.         The Davenport plant will utilize an electronic data base to compile process management tasks every week.  The database list contains the completed, activated, and on-going tasks at the plant. Each task contains a job description with the instructions and parts required to perform the specified maintenance procedures. The maintenance procedures can be updated weekly in the Electronic Database as needed.
4.         We also monitor and track contractors performance and safety records. This allows plant personnel to identify potential concerns with contractors awareness and knowledge of the ammonia process.
5.         The PSM coordinator and powerhouse planner meet with the Davenport Fire Dept annually to go over any changes or issues that have arose as well as response tra

ining.

E.  Five-year Accident History

The review of the Davenport facility's accident history includes the first day of production to present: June 7, 2017  June 17, 2025.  Our NAICS code is 311612   
1. October 10, 2024 6:27am - 9:30am 
	Anhydrous ammonia spill of approximately 5,000 pounds (concentration 100%)  
	Location - Power House Engine Room, from a condenser 
	Temp  46 degrees       Wind  6 mph,     West Humidity - 72%      Precipitation - 0
	Root cause was an oil line that broke on the compressor. There is a retro fit kit assembly to alleviate the cause of the failure on the line (oil tube separator to the oil block). We are testing this kit on the failed compressor, this will determine whether we change the line on the remaining compressors.
	The factory was evacuated; first shift employees were sent home. Davenport Fire Departments hazmat team responded and stayed onsite until the levels were permissible to enter.  Product on lines were tanked and all rooms went into sanitation.  Haz mat clean up team handled the engine room clean up, and the absorbents were sent to haz waste.  (No offsite impacts).
	Numerous changes in the powerhouse/engine room area have been made including: the retro fit kit on the bad piping, flange covers were installed on this piping on the compressors, installing windows in doors to engine room, changed programming of the fans to continue to run until turned off manually, additional inspections, ammonia ppm digital readouts on the outside of the building (engine room), making CCTVs assessable outside of the building, & remote ammonia alarms at security control center (some still in progress).
	The calculations for the release were done by Industrial Refrigeration Consortium. Level of accuracy = 100%

F.  Emergency Response Program

The Davenport facility has developed an emergency action plan, which complies with the OSHA standard and is comprised of 22 different sections that pertain to a proper response for the fac

ility. 

1. HAZWOPR 
2. SPCC/SWPP 
3. Fire Emergency 
4. Ammonia Release 
5. Bomb Threat 
6. Severe Weather 
7. Power Failure 
8. Evacuation
9. Manager listing 
10. Trained responders
11. First Aid Responders 
12. Emergency Communications 
13. Radio#, PH employees & Unit managers 
14. Response Checklists 
15. Stark St. Emergency Procedures 
16. Confined Space Program
17. Haz mat drills/critiques 
18. RMP
19. Emergency Response trailer checklist
20. Emergency Response training 
21. Emergency Response Bulk SDS
22. Freeze Prevention Plan
?
The combination of these 22 different documents yields a comprehensive Emergency Action Plan. Each section goes into detail about specifics needed for a proper response. The Emergency Response team will meet annually or when program changes occur to discuss updates to the emergency response plan. The entire Emergency Action Plan is updated at least annually. In addition, the emergency response team will do an annual ammonia response drill to practice for real life situations

As part of the emergency notification procedures, the Davenport Fire Department will be called to provide first emergency responders, equipment, and service.  The Davenport Fire Department will be called for all fire-related emergencies.  In all cases where the fire department is called, an ambulance will also be called to the scene.

This HAZWOPER and Emergency Action Plan addresses all the above mentioned procedures in detail.  This level of detail makes the emergency program at Kraft Heinz Davenport a thorough and comprehensive program.

G.  Planned Changes to Improve Safety 

Based on the what-if" Process Hazard Analysis completed pre-start up, a list of action items were developed and being monitored to determine if implementation was accomplished.  For example, if there is insufficient cooling to the condenser, the action item was to develop a PM to test controls annually. This recommendation was followed and is now an annual PM. There are numerous other

examples of safety improvements as a result of the PHA results.  These include but are not limited to the following:

1.         Bridges were installed on the roof to enable crossing over pipes when necessary

2.         Issue with dark areas were resolved by added lighting to condensers, roof and stairwells to roof

3.         Card swipes and keyed doors (interior & exterior) installed to the engine room and 
roof to ensure limited access to the area

4.         Two sets of stairs from ground to roof were added to the east and west sides of the facility for egress.
